newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Coffee drops after a spectacular rally.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Coffee drops after a spectacular rally.

text.p: World coffee markets have had a tumble after a spectacular rally that triggered retail price rises by leading U.S. and European brands.

Coffee futures prices, fuelled by tight supply of the arabica type of beans - the premium coffee - from South and Central America, had rocketed by more than 50 percent since early 1997 before beginning to come down this week.
The sudden decline surprised some analysts who thought arabica supply could remain tight well into the second half of 1997.
But most agree that the market could now take further falls if roasters (processors) finish an overdue rebuilding of low stocks and consumers resist the higher supermarket prices.
The price of May coffee on the New York futures for arabicas dropped as low as $1.65 per pound on Tuesday.
It had risen above $2.00 on March 5 for the first time since the last big crop-damaging frost in Brazil in 1994, rising from a cyclical low around $1.15 on January 2.
London's futures for robusta type beans, used mainly in the manufacture of solubles, fell almost five percent on Tuesday to $1,610 per tonne for the May contract.
While the coffee rally ran out of momentum, the cocoa market turned buoyant with London prices setting new seven-month highs on Tuesday.
Analysts said a shift of fund investments from coffee to cocoa could be the main driving factor. But although cocoa could rise further, prices are unlikely to rocket, traders said.
"It's not going to be coffee. One needs to be more cautious in cocoa. There isn't as much reason for the market to shoot up," one London trader said.
The rally in coffee was fuelled in part by forecasts of a lower Brazil crop and by supply disruptions in Colombia.
Market watchers said that, while a fall was inevitable as the market had been overbought, the question was how much more it could slide.
Immediately, New York's May could come down to the 160-cent level before retracing further to 150s.
"There could be some support below the market," said Neil Rosser, an analyst at UK trade house E D & F Man. "Roasters are more cautious now."

Until recently, roasters had been operating a hand-to-mouth buying policy based on holding minimal stocks but they were forced to replenish stocks and make extra purchases, helping to propel the rally, as values soared.
Leading brokerage GNI wondered on Tuesday how far coffee could fall before traders, roasters and speculators start buying again ahead of the Brazilian frost season in June and July.
The "bulls" are optimistic that coffee could climb back again based on what they see as sound supply fundamentals.
Tightness of good arabica coffee is expected to remain in the medium term as origin sellers have sold heavily in the last few weeks to cash in on the high prices, said one.
Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes in comments late last week said Brazilian weather and the size of Brazilian and Colombian crops would determine the direction of the market.

"If the market were to suddenly find that production in the top two countries is not as small as it now believes and there are no frost scares, the bulls' confidence might be shaken," she said. -- London newsroom +44 171 542 4985
